1302657500957806595 [2020-09-06] @DRMacIver 💜 17 [(SEED) type=semantic_search]
For any given book, you may want to read any percentage between 0 and 100% of the words in it. Skillfull reading is in large part about:

1) Deciding what the right percentage is.
2) Getting the most out of reading that percentage.
↓
1302657502396456960 [2020-09-06] @DRMacIver 💜 6
Sometimes when you're putting off reading a book it's because you're treating it as 100% book when actually it's only a 10% book for you right now.

This is partly prompted by me finally picking up Gabor Mate's "Scattered Minds", which I was definitely doing that to.
↓
1302657503851839488 [2020-09-06] @DRMacIver 💜 6 🔁 2
I'm somewhat ambivalent on the "some books should be essays". I think it's true that for most people and most books there is an essay that exists that would serve the book's purpose for them, but it's not always the same essay.
↓
1302657505231859713 [2020-09-06] @DRMacIver 💜 2
I think there's a lot to like in the 90% of the words in Scattered Minds that I'm not reading, and I may try a different sampling of it later where I engage with some of them properly, but they're not the words it would be useful for me to read at the moment.
↓
1302660695520153600 [2020-09-06] @DRMacIver 💜 2
The reason it's a 10% book for me BTW is that most of the 90% is autobiography and I've heard plenty of life stories from ADHD friends (plus my own not too dissimilar situation) and have no personal interest in Gabor Mate
↓
1302660837526601728 [2020-09-06] @DRMacIver 💜 4
"Too much of this book is an autobiography" is often the reason for low percentages.

1667587640529387523 [2023-06-10] @abhayance 💜 4
in my case there’s been a long standing fear of wasted effort - i only ever want to ˆbarelyˆ make it over hurdlesthis sort of “optimization” can’t support devotion to excellence, which requires you to stop worrying about “wasted effort” and focus on intensifying intentionality

1800161248287563935 [2024-06-10] @mbateman 💜 167 🔁 1
Btw the reason most people don’t “do the reading” is that it isn’t worth it for them to do so. It often takes a weird skill set to be able to reap value from “doing the reading”. In this case it’s carefully reading 1000+ pages of an obtuse vitalist who died in 1952. Like, why?
↓
1800162067451879629 [2024-06-10] @mbateman 💜 97
A tiny fraction of people has the patience or desire to parse out the historical context and/or find enough differences between her 1910s work and mostly similar 1920s work for it to be worthwhile for some idiosyncratic action context.
↓

A footnote: getting a humanities PhD is excellent training for this. I have a PhD in philosophy. This degree is widely considered professionally useless apart from academia, but I’ve found the training (if not the credential) immensely valuable in doing extra-academic work.

A memorable moment in new employee training for me was when the trainer said that most people working professionally in our field could not whiteboard out funds and data flow between all entities in a credit card transaction. She asked why I could, given no experience in industry https://t.co/K5kDmpNTAG
  [Quoting @visakanv: imo: if you’re deliberate about “doing the reading”, whatever that means for any domain, within a year it’s possible to be in the top ~5% in the scene. This is because 95% of people don’t do the reading https://t.co/cGLCJf3hQV]

1800163707730985191 [2024-06-10] @patio11 💜 816 🔁 14
The answer I gave was that I had credit card processing accounts before and read the documentation and contracts carefully. This was true, but was a bit of a fib.

The real reason was I was curious about how PayPal worked in 2004 and had some time to kill.
↓
1800164393050911047 [2024-06-10] @patio11 💜 1266 🔁 92
You’d be surprised what you can learn by reading more of the Internet than anyone thinks is reasonable.

You’d also be surprised how many people consider themselves cogs in a machine, with a bit of knowledge of what their gears touch and then no real interest beyond that.

I’d note that this is a strategy and it gets compounding effects when you e.g. use partial knowledge as a buy-in to get interesting conversations, move to parts of graph where you are exposed to more, etc.

if you want to know the classic texts in any field, just look for book recommendations from experts. Take note of any book that's repeatedly recommended. Books most/all mention are the classics, read them and the "core patterns" of the domain are often explicitly described

it's not just "pile of facts" about the domain, but it's the framing of how to approach the domain, and the patterns of what usually goes right and goes wrong. The classic texts almost always draw this out and cover it extensively, way beyond "pile of facts"
